content: Bowel preparation agents, when used in conjunction with drugs that induce Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion (SIADH) or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), can significantly increase the risk of water retention and electrolyte imbalances. This necessitates close monitoring of the patient. The combination of fluconazole and sodium sulfate/potassium chloride/magnesium sulfate/polyethylene glycol can lead to a reduction in serum potassium levels. Therapy should be modified or closely monitored in such cases. Fludrocortisone, when used with sodium sulfate/potassium chloride/magnesium sulfate/polyethylene glycol, also decreases serum potassium levels. Therapy adjustments or close monitoring are recommended. Fluoxetine, when combined with sodium sulfate/potassium chloride/magnesium sulfate/polyethylene glycol, requires caution and close monitoring due to potential interactions. Flurbiprofen, when co-administered with sodium sulfate/potassium chloride/magnesium sulfate/polyethylene glycol, should be used cautiously and monitored closely, as the combination may exacerbate risks associated with water retention or electrolyte disturbances. Fluvoxamine, when used with sodium sulfate/potassium chloride/magnesium sulfate/polyethylene glycol, also requires close monitoring due to the potential for increased water retention or electrolyte imbalances. All drug labels, including over-the-counter medications, should be carefully reviewed for PEG content. Common adverse effects of bowel preparation agents include nausea (7-13%), abdominal distension (1-6%), vomiting (4-6%), abdominal pain (3%), and headache (2-3%). Serious cardiovascular complications such as arrhythmias, atrial fibrillation, peripheral edema, asystole, and acute pulmonary edema have been reported. Gastrointestinal complications include upper gastrointestinal bleeding from Mallory-Weiss tears and esophageal perforation, often associated with gastroesophageal reflux.
